questions.q: In `process.argv`, what does index 2 (`process.argv[2]`) contain when you run `node check-balance.js 0xABC...`?
options: The Node executable path
The script file's path
The first real argument typed after the script name, e.g. "0xABC..."
Always undefined
questions.explain: process.argv[0] is the Node executable, [1] is the script path, and real arguments start at index 2 — so the address typed on the command line lands there.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend wrapping script logic in `async function main()` with a single `.catch()`, instead of using bare top-level await?
options: Bare top-level await is not valid JavaScript syntax
main() runs faster than top-level await

An uncaught rejection from bare top-level await can print a messy trace and, depending on the Node version, still leave the process exiting 0 — main().catch() gives one controlled place to log the error and set the exit code
Node does not support async functions
questions.explain: The main().catch() pattern centralizes error handling and lets the script reliably call process.exit(1) on failure, which a bare top-level await doesn't guarantee as cleanly.

questions.q: What does `process.exit(1)` signal to anything running or chaining this script (a shell, CI pipeline, or cron job)?
options: That the script succeeded
That the script failed — any nonzero exit code signals "something went wrong" to automated tooling
That the script is still running
It has no effect outside of a human reading console output
questions.explain: Automated tooling (CI, cron, shell && chains) decides what to do next based on the exit code, not printed output — 0 means success, any nonzero code signals failure.

questions.q: In the lesson's check-balance script, what happens if a user runs it with no address argument at all?
options: It silently uses a default address
process.argv[2] is undefined, so the script prints a usage message and exits with code 1 before trying to call getBalance
It throws an unrelated TypeScript compiler error
Node automatically prompts the user to type an address interactively
questions.explain: The script explicitly checks `if (!address)` and exits early with a usage message and a nonzero code, instead of letting `undefined` flow into provider.getBalance() and fail with a confusing error.

questions.q: What command from Lesson 32's npm patterns is used in this lesson to run the TypeScript script directly, without a separate compile step?
options: npm publish
tsx (e.g. `tsx src/check-balance.ts`), run directly or via npx
git commit
process.exit()
questions.explain: tsx runs a TypeScript file directly in development without a separate `tsc` compile step first, as introduced via npm scripts/npx in Lesson 32.
